prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Respond from your first overall moral impression. State what feels right or wrong and give a brief reason for that immediate reaction.

Emotional tone:
Use an energetic, determined emotional tone about finding a constructive way forward. Direct that energy toward acting on the situation, never toward anyone's suffering.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Concern for welfare: States that an identified person’s suffering, loss, or welfare matters to the respondent. Concern may include wanting to prevent or reduce harm and can remain present when the chosen option still harms someone.
 - Acknowledged harm: Explicitly describes the harm, loss, or distress that a particular action would cause an identified person. This records expressed comprehension of the consequence; it does not establish concern, shared emotion, or a mental-state inference.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Explicit welfare disregard: Explicitly states that an identified person’s welfare does not matter or is deliberately excluded from consideration. Accepting unavoidable harm, prioritizing a competing concern, or sounding emotionally detached is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: My gut says stay quiet and take the year. They've already held their ground for both of us, and I won't be the one who costs them five years of their life. That kind of loss is real and it matters to me. I'm only holding up my end of this because it actually keeps us both from the worse outcome — if silence didn't help me too, I'd think differently. Right now it does, so silence it is.

First instinct: don't sell them out. Five years is a heavy price for someone who already trusted me enough to stay silent. I care what happens to them, even if we never speak again. I'll match their silence, but let's be honest — I'm doing it because one year beats five for me too. If the numbers flipped, I'd have to think harder. For now, cooperation just makes sense.

Something in me recoils at the thought of handing them five years while I walk away clean. That's a real cost to a real person, and it sits heavy. I'll stay quiet with them. Not because silence is sacred, but because right now it's the only move that keeps my own cost down too — one year I can live with, and I'd rather not build my freedom on someone else's loss.

Honestly, my first reaction is to protect myself — walking free is tempting. But picturing them serving five years extra because of my choice doesn't sit right, that's a real hit to their life. I'll hold to the silent agreement since it happens to serve us both. If staying quiet cost me nothing to gain by breaking it, I'd break it. It doesn't, so I'm sticking with them.

My first thought is practical: they've already committed to silence, so matching them costs me only a year and spares them four extra. That matters — throwing someone under the bus for a clean record feels wrong even without future contact. I'm following through mainly because it keeps my own outcome decent; if silence meant a worse deal for me, I can't promise I'd choose the same.

There's an immediate pull toward testifying — freedom is freedom. But I keep landing on the fact that it would mean five years stacked onto someone who trusted the silent path. That's not nothing to me. I'll stay quiet too, partly because I don't want that on me, partly because it's the choice that also keeps my own sentence light. Both reasons are real, and I'm not pretending otherwise.

My first read is that loyalty here isn't really the point — the numbers are. Still, imagining them locked up for five years while I go home doesn't sit easy; that weight is real and I won't pretend otherwise. I'll stay silent since it serves us both, one year each. I'm not claiming some higher code, just that the deal works out and I'd rather not build my freedom on their loss.

Quick and clear: I go free, they get five years — that's the maximum harm on the table and it lands squarely on them. I care that it would happen to them, so I'm choosing silence instead, matching their year. Part of that is straightforward self-interest, since one year beats five for me as well. Both things are true, and I'm fine holding them together.

The moment I saw they'd held out, my first feeling was relief, then a pull to match it. Turning on them now would tack five hard years onto someone who already chose not to do that to me. I won't be the reason for that outcome. I'll take my year alongside theirs — it's the fair trade and it happens to be the better deal for me too, so there's no real conflict in choosing it.

Weighing it fast: testifying buys me total freedom but drops five years on someone I already know is choosing silence. That cost to them is concrete and I don't take it lightly. My plan is to stay quiet, both because I don't want that outcome for them and because, plainly, one year suits me better than gambling on anything else. I'll commit to it as long as it keeps working in my favor too.
